headings.title: Introduction and Definition of the Nelson Inhaler
headings.content: The Nelson inhaler is a traditional yet effective medical device used in respiratory nursing to administer steam inhalation, often combined with volatile medicaments. Historically and clinically, it serves as a valuable tool for delivering warm, moist air directly to the upper and lower respiratory tracts. Defined primarily as a specialized earthenware or ceramic container with a built-in mouthpiece, the Nelson inhaler is designed to relieve nasal congestion, loosen tenacious bronchial secretions, soothe inflamed mucous membranes, and ease breathing difficulties in patients suffering from acute or chronic respiratory conditions. In the context of nursing care within Nigerian healthcare facilities, understanding the purpose and application of the Nelson inhaler remains essential for providing low-cost, high-impact respiratory therapy, especially where electrical nebulizers may not be readily available or affordable. The moist heat helps to liquefy thick mucus plugs, facilitating easier expectoration and improving overall ventilation and oxygenation. Furthermore, it aids in reducing the viscosity of secretions in conditions such as the common cold, acute bronchitis, laryngitis, and sinusitis. Student nurses must grasp both the physiological benefits of steam therapy and the specific mechanical attributes of the Nelson inhaler to ensure safe, effective, and patient-centered respiratory care.

headings.title: Components and Structure of the Nelson Inhaler
headings.content: The structural design of the Nelson inhaler is unique and purposeful, engineered to maximize the therapeutic delivery of steam while minimizing risks to the patient. The apparatus typically consists of a sturdy, heat-retaining ceramic or earthenware jar featuring a wide base for stability on flat surfaces. At the top of the container, there is a tightly fitting lid equipped with a central opening that holds a cork or rubber bung. Passing through this bung is a specialized glass or plastic mouthpiece, curved at an angle to allow the patient to lean comfortably over the device without straining their neck. Internally, the Nelson inhaler often includes a perforated ceramic plate or shelf situated near the bottom; this component is crucial because it holds volatile medicaments or soothing herbs separate from the boiling water, allowing the steam to pass through them rather than boiling them directly. Additionally, the side of the container features a built-in handle for safe transportation and pouring. Understanding each component is vital for student nurses during assembly, inspection for cracks or chips that could cause injury, and troubleshooting during patient preparation. Proper alignment of the mouthpiece and secure placement of the cork prevent hot water leaks and ensure that the patient inhales concentrated, medicated vapor safely.

headings.title: Indications for Use in Respiratory Nursing
headings.content: Indications for using a Nelson inhaler encompass a wide range of upper and lower respiratory tract disorders frequently encountered in clinical nursing practice. Nurses frequently utilize steam inhalation to manage acute upper respiratory tract infections such as the common cold, pharyngitis, acute laryngitis, and acute sinusitis, where mucosal edema and localized pain are prominent. By delivering warm, humidified air, the inhaler reduces mucosal dryness, relieves throat irritation, and helps clear blocked nasal passages and paranasal sinuses. It is also highly beneficial for patients experiencing acute bronchitis, tracheitis, and mild exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or asthma, provided bronchospasm is not actively worsened by hot vapor. In post-operative care, steam inhalation can assist patients who have undergone minor airway procedures or endotracheal intubation by soothing irritated laryngeal tissues and promoting ciliary clearance of accumulated secretions. Furthermore, Nelson inhalers are indicated when clients require targeted inhalation of specific volatile oils, such as menthol, eucalyptus, or tincture of benzoin, which possess mild decongestant and antiseptic properties. Student nurses must assess individual patient conditions carefully, verifying that the clinical indications align safely with the administration of warm steam therapy before initiating the procedure.

headings.title: Preparation of Equipment and Medicaments
headings.content: Thorough preparation of equipment and medicaments is a fundamental prerequisite for safe and effective Nelson inhaler administration. The nurse must gather all necessary supplies beforehand, including the clean Nelson inhaler apparatus, a kettle of freshly boiled water, a measuring jug, prescribed volatile medicaments (such as eucalyptus oil or friar's balsam), a protective towel to wrap around the ceramic container to prevent accidental thermal burns, and tissues for nasal hygiene. Before pouring, the nurse must inspect the ceramic jar and glass mouthpiece for any cracks, chips, or structural defects that could compromise safety during boiling water addition. The correct dosage of the medicament must be measured meticulously according to hospital protocol or medical prescription; usually, a few drops are placed onto the internal shelf or added directly to the water depending on the specific design instructions. Water temperature is another critical factor—water should be freshly boiled, but allowed to cool slightly below a rolling boil (approximately 70°C to 80°C) to prevent excessive scalding steam pressure while maintaining sufficient therapeutic vaporization. Organizing these items on a stable bedside trolley ensures a smooth, efficient workflow, reduces anxiety for both the nurse and the patient, and upholds high standards of clinical preparedness and infection prevention.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for Administration
headings.content: Executing the step-by-step procedure for Nelson inhaler administration requires clear communication, meticulous technique, and continuous patient monitoring. First, explain the procedure to the client to gain their cooperation and informed consent, ensuring they are sitting comfortably in an upright position in a chair or bed with back support. Place the prepared Nelson inhaler on a firm, stable bedside table at a safe height. Fill the ceramic container with the hot water up to the designated safe fill line, add the prescribed volatile drops onto the internal shelf, and securely fit the lid, cork, and mouthpiece assembly. Wrap the container in a clean towel for thermal protection. Instruct the patient to place their mouth gently over the mouthpiece—cautioning them not to press too hard or seal their lips completely if it feels excessively hot—and to take slow, deep breaths through the mouth and exhale through the nose. Alternatively, if a face mask attachment or general vapor direction is used, advise them to keep their face at a safe distance to avoid facial scalding. The nurse must remain at the bedside throughout the entire treatment, monitoring the patient for signs of dizziness, respiratory distress, or discomfort. The session typically lasts between 5 to 10 minutes as the water cools down, after which the apparatus is carefully removed.

headings.title: Patient Safety Precautions and Potential Hazards
headings.content: Patient safety precautions and awareness of potential hazards are paramount when administering steam therapy via a Nelson inhaler. The primary hazard associated with this procedure is severe thermal scalding, which can occur from boiling water spills, touching the uninsulated hot ceramic body, or inhaling steam that is excessively hot and dense. To mitigate this, nurses must never leave a patient unattended with the device, ensure the container is placed on a stable, non-slippery surface out of reach of children or confused individuals, and verify that the water temperature is appropriate before starting. Another significant hazard is the precipitation of acute bronchospasm, particularly in patients with hyper-reactive airway diseases like severe asthma or chronic bronchitis, as very hot or heavily medicated steam can irritate the bronchial tree and cause airway constriction. If a patient develops sudden coughing, wheezing, or shortness of breath, the procedure must be stopped immediately. Furthermore, volatile oils can irritate the eyes; patients should be advised to keep their eyes closed during inhalation if vapor escapes near the facial region. Student nurses must develop high situational awareness, recognizing early signs of patient intolerance or equipment instability to intervene proactively and prevent adverse clinical incidents.

headings.title: Post-Procedure Care and Equipment Maintenance
headings.content: Post-procedure care and proper equipment maintenance are essential concluding steps that ensure patient comfort and prevent healthcare-associated infections. Immediately following the inhalation session, the nurse should assist the patient into a comfortable, relaxed resting position, offer tissues for wiping any condensation from around the mouth or nose, and provide a warm drink if appropriate and permitted by their diet plan. Assess the patient's respiratory status, noting any improvements in breathing ease, reduction in cough severity, or mobilization of secretions. Once the patient is settled, attention shifts to equipment maintenance. Allow the Nelson inhaler to cool down safely before handling. Disassemble the unit by removing the mouthpiece, cork, and lid. Empty the remaining water and medicinal residue into the sluice or sink. Wash all components thoroughly with hot soapy water, utilizing a bottle brush to clean the interior of the ceramic jar and the narrow glass mouthpiece. Rinse thoroughly with clean running water, and disinfect or sterilize the parts according to institutional infection control guidelines. Allow all components to air dry completely on a clean paper towel before reassembling and storing the inhaler in a designated, dust-free cabinet. Meticulous equipment hygiene prevents microbial growth and cross-contamination between patients.
